key_terms.meaning: The system is the quantity of matter or region chosen for study; the boundary (control surface) is the real or imaginary surface that separates it from the surroundings
A system of fixed mass; no mass crosses the boundary, though heat and work may
A region of fixed location through which mass may flow in and out
A system that exchanges neither mass nor energy (heat or work) with the surroundings
A system whose properties are the same at every point, e.g. a single gas phase
A system with more than one phase or region, so properties jump at interfaces
A property independent of the size of the system, e.g. T, P, density ρ, molar volume v
A property proportional to the amount of matter, e.g. mass m, volume V, total internal energy U; dividing by mass gives a specific property
An extensive property divided by the number of moles n, e.g. molar volume v = V/n in m³/mol
A property fixed once the state is fixed; its change depends only on the end states, e.g. U, H, T, P
A quantity whose value depends on the route between the end states, e.g. work W and heat Q
An ideal process that proceeds through a continuous series of equilibrium states and can be reversed exactly by an infinitesimal change in the surroundings
Any real process with friction, finite gradients or unrestrained expansion, so it cannot be reversed without extra work input from outside
Energy in transition across the boundary due to a driving force and a displacement; for a simple compressible system δW = P dV
Energy in transition across the boundary because of a temperature difference; δQ is not an exact differential
If A is in thermal equilibrium with C and B is in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and B are in equilibrium with each other; this makes temperature a property
An adiabatic wall blocks heat transfer; a diathermal wall allows heat transfer so that equilibrium can be reached

key_terms.term: First law for a closed system
key_terms.meaning: ΔU = Q − W for a change of state, and ∮δQ = ∮δW for a cycle; U is a state function
For an open system at steady state with one inlet and one outlet: Q − W<sub>s</sub> = ΔH + Δ(v²/2) + Δ(gz) per unit mass
Flow work Pv is the work done to push fluid in and out; adding it to internal energy gives enthalpy H = U + PV
C<sub>v</sub> = (∂U/∂T)<sub>v</sub> and C<sub>p</sub> = (∂H/∂T)<sub>p</sub>, in J/(mol·K) or kJ/(kg·K)
Ducts that convert enthalpy into kinetic energy (nozzle, pressure falls) or kinetic energy into enthalpy (diffuser, pressure rises); both are nearly adiabatic with no shaft work

takeaways: A thermodynamic system is defined only after you draw the boundary; every balance is written for what crosses that boundary.
Intensive properties locate the state; extensive properties scale with amount and become specific or molar properties after dividing by mass or moles.
State functions depend only on where you start and end; work and heat depend on the road taken between them.
Energy is stored as internal, kinetic or potential energy, or is in transit as heat or work; only transit terms cross the boundary.
The zeroth law is what makes temperature measurable, and the ideal-gas scale lets any gas thermometer agree with the rest.
ΔU = Q − W for a closed system is the whole first law; Joule's paddle-wheel experiment is what tells us U is a state function.
Enthalpy is not a new kind of energy, only U + PV, and it enters open-system balances because the fluid carries flow work in and out.
C<sub>v</sub> and C<sub>p</sub> convert temperature changes into internal-energy and enthalpy changes; for an ideal gas C<sub>p</sub> − C<sub>v</sub> = R.
In a nozzle the energy of the flow is still conserved, but enthalpy converts into kinetic energy, so pressure and temperature both fall.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to combine a clean statement of the law with a labelled control volume, a correctly signed energy balance and a numerical substitution in consistent units; definitions and classifications carry easy marks, so start with them.

bank.q: Define a thermodynamic system and its boundary. Distinguish closed, open and isolated systems and give one plant example of each. Classify these as intensive or extensive: pressure, volume, molar volume, density, temperature, total enthalpy, mass, specific heat capacity.
outline: System = whatever lies inside the chosen boundary; boundary is real or imaginary
Closed: fixed mass, energy may cross (piston-cylinder gas)
Open: mass crosses (pump, heat exchanger, turbine)
Isolated: neither mass nor energy crosses (perfectly insulated rigid vessel)
Intensive: pressure, temperature, density, molar volume, specific heat capacity
Extensive: volume, mass, total enthalpy
Dividing an extensive property by mass or moles gives a specific or molar (intensive) property

bank.q: State the zeroth law of thermodynamics and show how it leads to temperature as a property. Describe the constant-volume gas thermometer and explain why the ideal-gas temperature scale does not depend on which gas is used.
outline: Statement of transitivity of thermal equilibrium
Diathermal wall lets systems reach equilibrium; adiabatic wall prevents it
Equilibrium means no observable change and a common value of the property called temperature
Constant-volume gas thermometer: P vs T at fixed V, T = 273.16 × (P/P<sub>tp</sub>) K
All gases give the same limiting value as P → 0, which defines the ideal-gas scale
Relation to Celsius and Kelvin offsets; fixed points (ice point, steam point, triple point)

bank.q: Distinguish point functions from path functions with examples. Explain what an exact differential is and use it to show that work and heat are not properties of a system.
outline: Point function: fixed by state, change independent of path, has an exact differential
Path function: depends on route, written δW and δQ, no exact differential
Example: 1 kg gas from state 1 to state 2 by different routes gives different W and Q
∮dU = 0 for a cycle, but ∮δQ = ∮δW ≠ 0
Consequence: U, H, T, P can be tabulated; W and Q cannot

bank.q: State the first law of thermodynamics for a closed system undergoing a cycle and for a closed system undergoing a change of state. Describe Joule's paddle-wheel experiment and explain what it proves about internal energy.
outline: Cycle: ∮δQ = ∮δW, so net heat equals net work
Change of state: ΔU = Q − W with sign convention
Joule's experiment: falling weights drive a paddle, insulated vessel of water, measured work and temperature rise
Same temperature rise is produced by a different amount of work or by heating — the mechanical equivalent of heat
Conclusion: U is a state function; the energy change depends only on end states, not on whether work or heat caused it
Limitations of Joule's original measurement and why a state function is needed

bank.q: Define internal energy and enthalpy. Derive the constant-volume and constant-pressure heat capacities from the first law and relate C<sub>p</sub>, C<sub>v</sub> and R for an ideal gas.
outline: U is the energy stored at molecular level; absolute value unknown, changes are computed
H = U + PV, a state function, useful for constant-pressure processes
At constant volume, W = 0, so δQ = dU and C<sub>v</sub> = (∂U/∂T)<sub>v</sub>
At constant pressure, δQ = dH and C<sub>p</sub> = (∂H/∂T)<sub>p</sub>
For an ideal gas, U and H depend on T only, so dU = C<sub>v</sub>dT and dH = C<sub>p</sub>dT
C<sub>p</sub> − C<sub>v</sub> = R per mole; γ = C<sub>p</sub>/C<sub>v</sub>

bank.q: A rigid, insulated vessel holds 2 kg of a gas at 300 K. A paddle wheel does 60 kJ of work on the gas while a heater inside supplies 25 kJ. Find ΔU and the final temperature if C<sub>v</sub> = 0.75 kJ/(kg·K).
outline: Rigid vessel: W<sub>boundary</sub> = 0; only paddle work crosses
First law with sign conventions: ΔU = Q − W = +25 − (−60)
ΔU = 85 kJ
ΔU = m C<sub>v</sub> ΔT → ΔT = 85/(2 × 0.75) = 56.7 K
Final temperature 356.7 K
Note that both heat and work inputs raise U; state convention clearly

bank.q: Steam at 1 MPa and 300 °C enters an insulated nozzle at 40 m/s and leaves at 0.2 MPa with negligible velocity change. Taking enthalpies 3051 kJ/kg and 2769 kJ/kg, find the exit velocity.
outline: Steady-flow energy equation with Q = 0 and W<sub>s</sub> = 0
h<sub>1</sub> + v<sub>1</sub>²/2 = h<sub>2</sub> + v<sub>2</sub>²/2 (z terms cancelled)
Convert kJ/kg to J/kg before adding kinetic energy terms
h<sub>1</sub> − h<sub>2</sub> = 282 × 10³ J/kg
v<sub>2</sub>² = v<sub>1</sub>² + 2 × 282000; v<sub>1</sub>² = 1600 m²/s²
v<sub>2</sub> ≈ 752 m/s; comment on why nozzles are nearly adiabatic

bank.q: A compressor takes air at 100 kPa and 300 K at 90 m/s and delivers it at 500 kPa and 460 K at 20 m/s. The mass flow rate is 0.05 kg/s and heat loss is 3 kW. Find the shaft power required, taking C<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 kJ/(kg·K).
outline: Steady-flow equation: Q − W<sub>s</sub> = m[(h<sub>2</sub> − h<sub>1</sub>) + (v<sub>2</sub>² − v<sub>1</sub>²)/2 + gΔz]
Δh = C<sub>p</sub>ΔT = 1.005 × 160 = 160.8 kJ/kg
Kinetic term (400 − 8100)/2 = −3850 J/kg = −3.85 kJ/kg
Per kg: Q/m = −3/0.05 = −60 kJ/kg
Power = 0.05 × 216.95 ≈ 10.8 kW input; negative sign means work on the system

bank.q: One mole of an ideal gas at 300 K and 1 bar is heated to 500 K, first at constant volume and then at constant pressure. With C<sub>v</sub> = 20.8 J/(mol·K) and R = 8.314 J/(mol·K), compute Q, W and ΔU for both paths and compare.
outline: Constant volume: W = 0, Q = ΔU = C<sub>v</sub>ΔT = 4160 J
Constant pressure: C<sub>p</sub> = C<sub>v</sub> + R = 29.114; Q = 5823 J
ΔU same for both paths = 4160 J because U is a state function
W = Q − ΔU = 1663 J = RΔT
Difference in Q equals the extra PV work
Plot both paths on a P–V diagram to show equal ΔU, different area

bank.q: A gas in a piston-cylinder assembly expands from 2 bar and 0.1 m³ to 0.3 m³. Compute the work done when the expansion is (a) isobaric, (b) isothermal, (c) against vacuum, and state which is the maximum for reversible isothermal expansion.
outline: Sign convention: work done by the system is positive, W = ∫P dV
Isobaric: W = P(V<sub>2</sub> − V<sub>1</sub>) = 200 × 0.2 = 40 kJ
Isothermal: W = P<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> ln(V<sub>2</sub>/V<sub>1</sub>) = 20 × ln 3 = 21.97 kJ
Against vacuum: P<sub>ext</sub> = 0, so W = 0
Reversible isothermal gives the maximum work between two states
The three answers show W is a path function

bank.q: Derive the steady-flow energy equation for an open system and explain why enthalpy appears in it while the closed-system balance uses internal energy. Show that the flow-work term Pv is the reason for the shift.
outline: Take a control volume, apply conservation of mass and of energy over a time interval
Work terms: shaft work W<sub>s</sub> plus work done by the fluid on the fluid ahead (flow work Pv)
E<sub>in</sub> − E<sub>out</sub> = ΔU + ΔKE + ΔPE per unit mass plus flow work
Combine u + Pv = h
Q − W<sub>s</sub> = ΔH + Δ(v²/2) + gΔz
For a closed system the boundary moves with the mass so Pv terms cancel
Check limiting cases: no flow gives ΔU = Q − W; Q = W<sub>s</sub> = 0 in a nozzle gives h<sub>1</sub> + v<sub>1</sub>²/2 = h<sub>2</sub> + v<sub>2</sub>²/2

bank.q: A student argues: since Q and W depend on the path, the first law ΔU = Q − W means internal energy must also depend on the path. Examine this argument and explain what makes ΔU path-independent. Include a cyclic process in your answer.
outline: Identify the error: Q and W change together so their difference is path-independent
State exact-differential test for dU versus δQ and δW
Illustrate with two paths between the same states: different Q, different W, same ΔU
Cycle: ∮dU = 0 while ∮δQ = ∮δW ≠ 0
Joule's experiment as experimental evidence
Consequence: property tables and equations of state are possible
Strength/limitation: first law alone does not say which direction a process can go — that needs the second law

bank.q: Compare a throttling valve, a nozzle and a compressor as steady-flow devices. For each, write the reduced energy equation, state the assumptions and explain where the energy goes.
outline: All three: steady flow, single inlet and outlet, neglect ΔPE
Throttling: Q = 0, W = 0, ΔKE ≈ 0 → h<sub>1</sub> = h<sub>2</sub>, isenthalpic; pressure drops through friction, irreversible
Nozzle: Q = 0, W = 0 → enthalpy converts into kinetic energy, pressure and temperature fall
Compressor: ΔKE small, Q small → W<sub>s</sub> ≈ Δh, work input raises pressure and enthalpy
Identify which terms may be dropped and why; mention typical assumptions of negligible heat loss
Compare reversibility: nozzle and diffuser designed near-isentropic, throttling fully irreversible

bank.q: Choose a control volume for a steam turbine in a power plant and carry out a full energy accounting for it. Discuss which terms you may neglect, how you would estimate the heat loss, and what the first law alone cannot tell you about the turbine's performance.
outline: Draw the control volume around the turbine casing with inlet, outlet and shaft
Write Q − W<sub>s</sub> = m[Δh + ΔKE + ΔPE]
Neglect ΔPE; check whether ΔKE is significant against Δh
Shaft work from the enthalpy drop; sign convention for work out
Estimate casing heat loss from insulation and surface temperature, show it is small but not zero
First law gives quantity of work only, not the best possible work — need the second law and isentropic efficiency
Practical points: steam quality at exit, condensate, unit consistency

bank.q: An insulated rigid tank is divided into two parts by a partition; one side holds a compressed gas and the other is evacuated. The partition is removed and the gas fills the tank. Analyse the process using the first law, state the assumptions, and comment on whether the gas temperature changes for an ideal gas.
outline: Closed system, rigid: W = 0; insulated: Q = 0 → ΔU = 0
Free expansion is highly irreversible, not a reversible adiabatic path
For an ideal gas U depends on T only, so T is unchanged and P falls as V increases
For a real gas, U depends on V too, so T changes (Joule coefficient)
Contrast with reversible adiabatic expansion where T falls
Note that the energy balance gives the answer without knowing the intermediate states

glossary.def: No heat crosses the boundary, Q = 0.
The surface, real or imaginary, that separates the system from its surroundings and across which heat, work and mass are counted.
A system of fixed mass in which no mass crosses the boundary.
A fixed region in space, with mass able to flow in and out, used for open-system analysis.
A wall that allows heat to pass so that two bodies can reach thermal equilibrium.
H = U + PV, a state function convenient for constant-pressure and flow processes.
A property proportional to the quantity of matter, such as mass, volume or total internal energy.
The Pv work a flowing fluid does on the fluid ahead of it and receives from the fluid behind it.
Energy transferred across a boundary because of a temperature difference.
The heat needed to raise the temperature of a unit amount by one kelvin, at constant volume or constant pressure.
A property independent of size, such as temperature, pressure or density.
The total kinetic and potential energy of the molecules of the system, a state function whose changes are measurable.
A real process with friction, finite gradients or unrestrained expansion that cannot be undone without external work.
A system that exchanges neither mass nor energy with the surroundings.
The SI base unit of thermodynamic temperature, defined by setting the triple point of water at 273.16 K.
An extensive property divided by the number of moles, in units per mole.
A duct of decreasing area in which pressure falls and velocity rises, with enthalpy converting to kinetic energy.
A system in which mass crosses the boundary, also called a control volume.
A quantity whose value between two states depends on the route, such as heat and work.
An idealised process through continuous equilibrium states that can be reversed exactly by an infinitesimal change in the surroundings.
An extensive property divided by mass, in units per kilogram.
A property fixed by the state of the system, so its change depends only on the end states.
A flow in which properties at any point do not change with time, so mass and energy within the control volume stay constant.
If two bodies are each in thermal equilibrium with a third, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other, which justifies temperature as a property.
